# ADR 0008 — Three gate stages, every gate proven by a probe, and tests chosen per layer

> **In short.** In the context of a repo whose rules are held by hooks, gates and tests from the first commit,
> facing gates that can pass because they check nothing, we decided for three stages without a warning level, a
> registered probe for every gate, and a fixed kind of test per layer of the hexagon, and against a single gate at
> the end and against trusting a green run, to know that every check can fail and does fail where it should,
> accepting that every new gate costs a probe before it may run.

## Context and problem

The setup of Pixecutive enforces its rules through hooks in `.claude/hooks/`, git hooks in `.githooks/` and gates in
`scripts/check-*.ts` ([ADR 0001](0001-one-carrier-per-rule.md)). A gate that never turns red looks exactly like a
gate that is kept: both exit with 0. A gate that reports things that are not violations is worse; it teaches
everyone to ignore it.

Product code arrives with PIX-7 in a strict hexagon: a framework-free core with ports, adapters in a separate
package, apps as composition roots. Each layer can be tested in a different way, and choosing the wrong one makes
tests slow or makes them test a stub instead of the code.

## Decision drivers

- A violation must be visible at the earliest point that can see it.
- A gate must prove that it can fail; a green run is not a yes.
- A gate with false alarms is worse than none.
- Tests must check real code, and the core must be testable without infrastructure.

## Considered options

- **A — Three stages, a probe per gate, tests per layer.**
- **B — One full gate before the pull request.**
- **C — A full gate after every write**, including type check and all tests.

## Decision

Chosen: **A**, because B finds a violation long after it was written, and C slows every write and fails on every
intermediate state.

1. **Three stages, and red is red.** Hooks check the touched file on every write; pre-commit checks the staged
   state; the full verify runs before every push. There is no warning level.
   `[Hook quality-guard · Hook pre-commit · Hook pre-push]`
2. **Every gate has a probe** that plants a violation and turns the gate red, then turns it green on the fixed
   state. Every probe is registered in `.claude/data/precommit-checks.tsv`; pre-commit rejects a probe that is not
   registered. A gate is wired into pre-commit only after its probe turned red and green.
   `[Hook pre-commit · Config precommit-checks.tsv]`
3. **A gate with false alarms is switched off, not obeyed.** A new check is first held against a state known to be
   correct; if it reports anything there, the check is wrong, not the code. `[Prose: whether a finding is a false
   alarm is decided by reading it, not by the gate that raised it]`
4. **A violation a gate should have caught is a hole in the gate.** The finding is the check that stayed silent,
   not the place. `[Config precommit-checks.tsv]`
5. **Tests per layer.** Pure domain functions are tested directly. Use cases are tested with hand-written in-memory
   fakes that implement the port. Adapters have unit specs and integration specs; the integration specs are skipped
   when no database URL is set. `[Planned PIX-7: Gate full verify with Vitest · Agent adversarial-review]`

### Consequences

- Good, because a violation is reported on the write that caused it, not at the pull request.
- Good, because every green gate has once been seen red, so green means "checked and kept", not "not checked".
- Good, because use-case tests need no infrastructure; the fake implements the same port as the adapter.
- Bad, because every new gate costs a probe and a registration before it may run in pre-commit.
- Bad, because integration specs are skipped on a machine without a database URL, so a local green run does not
  cover them.
- A green run is not a yes: a gate says nothing measurable is broken, not that the thing works. The verdict comes
  from the maintainer or a measurement.

### Confirmation

pre-commit lists the probes in `.claude/data/precommit-checks.tsv` and runs each; a probe file that exists without a
row is rejected, and a planted unregistered probe proves that rejection. `quality-guard` turns red on a planted
violation in a touched file. `pre-push` turns red when the full verify fails. Each gate named in the other ADRs has
its own row.

## Mechanics

No diagram. The three stages are a sequence of three checks, listed in point 1.

## Rejected

- **B — one gate before the pull request.** Finds a violation long after it was written, when it is mixed into
  other changes.
- **C — the full gate after every write.** Slows every write and fails on every intermediate state.
- **A warning level.** A finding that does not fail is read once and then ignored.
- **Trusting a gate without a probe.** A gate that cannot turn red is indistinguishable from one that is kept.
